Psychology Today alternatives: the therapist directories worth knowing

Psychology Today is where most therapists list first, and for good reason: it is the directory most clients have heard of. It is not the only one, and depending on who you want to see and how you want to be paid, another directory, or a second one alongside it, may serve you better. This is a plain description of the main options, including Theraglee, with how to choose between them.

Why therapists look beyond Psychology Today

Psychology Today is the largest therapist directory in the United States and the one with the most name recognition among clients. As of October 2026 it costs about $30 a month, and credentials on it are self-reported rather than checked against a licensing board. Prices change, so check its current page.

Therapists go looking for alternatives for a few recurring reasons. In large cities, the list of therapists for any search is long and a new profile sits far down it. Some want a directory that reaches a particular community, whether a cultural or identity group, people who need reduced fees, or people who want a vetted therapist rather than a long list. Some want to stop paying a flat fee for a listing that has gone quiet. And some want a directory where the client comes to them rather than the reverse. None of the directories below replaces Psychology Today for everyone; each does something it does not.

Free listings: TherapyDen and Open Path Collective

TherapyDen is a free directory with a social-justice orientation. Its search filters go further than most on identity and values, so a client can look for therapists by, for instance, their stance on particular social issues or their experience with particular communities. If you want to be found by clients who care about those things, it is a strong fit, and the cost of a listing is only your time. Check its site for anything that has changed.

Open Path Collective is a nonprofit that connects people who cannot afford standard fees with therapists who offer a set number of reduced-fee slots. It is not a general marketing channel; you join to offer affordable care, and in return you reach clients who would not otherwise find you. Many therapists keep one or two Open Path slots as the sliding-scale part of their practice. Check its site for the current terms for therapists.

Paid general directories: GoodTherapy and psychology.com

GoodTherapy is a paid directory whose distinguishing feature is an ethics pledge therapists agree to when they list, built around collaborative, non-pathologizing care. Its client-facing articles on finding and understanding therapy bring in people who are researching before they book. Check its site for current pricing.

psychology.com is a general directory that, as of October 2026, charges $49 a month or $490 a year and checks listings against the NPI registry and the state board, with the check dated on the profile. It is a similar proposition to Psychology Today at a higher price, with verification as the difference. Prices change; check its current page.

Curated and identity-affirming directories: Zencare and Inclusive Therapists

Zencare is a curated directory available in select cities. Therapists are interviewed before they are listed, profiles include a video introduction, and the client-facing experience is designed around that vetting. If you practice in a city Zencare covers and you are comfortable on camera, it reaches clients who specifically want a screened list. Check its site for the cities it serves and its current fees.

Inclusive Therapists is an identity-affirming directory centered on clients from marginalized communities, with listing fees on a sliding scale so therapists at different income levels can take part. Its filters emphasize lived experience, cultural background and affirming practice. If that is the community you serve, it reaches clients that general directories do not. Check its site for current fees.

Insurance platforms that also list you: Headway and Alma

Headway and Alma are not directories in the traditional sense. They are platforms that credential you with insurers, handle billing and claims, and list you to clients searching within their systems. For a therapist who wants to take insurance without running the paperwork, that bundle is the appeal, and the listing is a side effect of it.

The cost model is the thing to understand. Headway is free to join, and as of October 2026 charges $9.99 per session for clients found through Headway, for the whole client relationship, a fee it announced that month. Alma's terms are different; check its current page for what it charges. In both cases, you are trading a share of session revenue, or a membership fee, for credentialing and billing you would otherwise do yourself. Our guide to directory costs works through what a per-session fee adds up to over a client relationship. Prices on both platforms change.

Theraglee

Theraglee is a newer directory built by a licensed therapist. Every listing is verified against the state licensing board before it goes live. The membership is one flat rate, $29 a month or $290 a year, with no per-session or per-contact fees, and it includes a protected Theraglee phone number that forwards to your real one, messages that never expose your email, referral stats on your dashboard, and a clinician library of worksheets and exercises that grows daily.

The feature that makes it different is Theraglee Match Mode: members who want a therapist to reach out flip a switch and appear on the dashboards of therapists whose listings fit them, pseudonymously, with an age range, gender, broad topics, who the sessions are for, in-person or video preference, insurance and the first three digits of their zip code. You send one message; the member replies with their real name only if they choose. Member data is never sold, never used for ads and never used to train AI. A founding offer runs for the first 150 spots through December 31, 2026: free until your first member match, then $20 a month locked in.

How to choose

Ask four questions of any directory before you pay for it or spend an evening building a profile.

  • Who searches here? A directory is worth exactly the clients it reaches. General directories reach the most people; community and curated directories reach fewer people who are a closer fit.
  • What does it really cost? A flat fee is predictable. A per-session fee is small per session and large over a client relationship. A free listing costs the time to maintain it.
  • Does it verify? Verification protects the directory's reputation and yours, and clients increasingly notice.
  • Who does the finding? Most directories wait for a client to search. A few, Theraglee among them, show you people who have asked to be contacted.

Then pick two, not six. Build each profile properly, with the same specialty line and the same photo, keep fees and openings current, and after six months look at where your new clients actually came from. Keep what worked. Cancel what did not.

Common questions

What is the best alternative to Psychology Today for therapists?

It depends on who you want to reach. TherapyDen is free and values-oriented, Zencare is curated in select cities, Inclusive Therapists serves marginalized communities, Open Path reaches clients who need reduced fees, Headway and Alma bundle insurance billing, and Theraglee is a flat-rate, license-verified directory where matched members can ask you to reach out.

Are there free therapist directories?

Yes. TherapyDen is free to list on, and Open Path Collective is a nonprofit you join to offer reduced-fee slots. Headway is free to join but, as of October 2026, charges $9.99 per session for clients found through it.

Should I list on more than one directory?

Two done well is usually the right number: one general directory and one that reaches the clients you most want. Build each profile fully, keep it current, and after six months keep what brought clients and cancel what did not.

How is Theraglee different from Psychology Today?

Theraglee verifies every license against the state board before a listing goes live, charges one flat rate of $29 a month or $290 a year with no per-session fees, and lets members who want a therapist to reach out appear on your dashboard through Match Mode. Psychology Today, as of October 2026, costs about $30 a month and relies on clients searching.
